rite: St Leo the Great was Pope from 440 to 461. His letter on the two natures of Christ, the Tome to Flavian, was read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and he went out in person to meet Attila the Hun in 452 to plead for Italy. He is a Doctor of the Church. His Christmas sermons echo today’s first reading.
study: Titus 2 gives teaching to old and young, men and women. Which part speaks most to my stage of life?
When do I expect God to owe me something for my prayers or my good works?

lead: Paul reminds Titus what Christians once were and what God has done: “he saved us … through the water of rebirth”. In the Gospel ten lepers are healed, but only one, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks. Baptism and the Eucharist meet here: we are washed by mercy, and the right answer to mercy is thanksgiving.

r.h: The water of rebirth
set: Paul ends his instructions to Titus with how Christians should live in society: obedient to lawful authority, ready for good work, gentle to all. The reason is not social respectability but memory: we too were once lost, and God saved us by mercy.
str: vv. 1–2: conduct towards rulers and neighbours.
v. 3: what we once were.
vv. 4–7: what God did: a short hymn of salvation, naming the Father, Christ and the Holy Spirit.
kw: God’s love for humankind. Greek kings boasted of their philanthropy; Paul gives the title to God.
A clear reference to Baptism: a washing that gives new birth (compare John 3:5).
Those who receive an inheritance as children of the house. Baptism makes us heirs of eternal life.
vv: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared,
he saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
Salvation is pure mercy. Our works follow it; they do not buy it.
ch: The Catechism uses these words as one of the names of Baptism: “the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1215). The whole Trinity is at work in vv. 4–7: the Father’s kindness, the Spirit poured out, through Jesus Christ our Savior.

r.h: The one who turned back
set: Jesus is travelling along the border between Samaria and Galilee. Lepers had to live apart and call out from a distance (Leviticus 13:45–46). Only a priest could declare them clean and allow them back into the community (Leviticus 14).
str: vv. 11–13: ten lepers cry for mercy from a distance.
v. 14: “Go and show yourselves to the priests”; on the way, they are made clean.
vv. 15–16: one turns back, praises God and falls at Jesus’ feet: a Samaritan.
vv. 17–19: Jesus’ questions and his word: “your faith has made you well.”
kw: A rare word. It is the word used on the stone notices in the Temple that forbade foreigners to go beyond the outer court. The one counted an outsider is the one who comes back to praise God.
The root of our word “Eucharist”. The Samaritan’s thanksgiving at Jesus’ feet is a picture of the Church’s worship.
vv: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice.
All ten were cleansed; one saw. Seeing what God has done is the start of thanksgiving.
Then he said to him, “Get up and go on your way; your faith has made you well.”
The Greek verb also means “has saved you”. The nine were healed in body; the Samaritan received more.
ch: The Catechism teaches that every event and need can become an offering of thanksgiving (CCC 2638), and that the Eucharist is above all thanksgiving to the Father (CCC 1360). At Mass we are invited to be the one who turns back.

rite: St Martin of Tours (died 397) was a soldier and still a catechumen when, at Amiens, he cut his cloak in half for a freezing beggar. His biographer Sulpicius Severus tells that Christ appeared to him that night wearing the half cloak, and that Martin then asked for Baptism (in substance). He became a monk and then Bishop of Tours. Today’s two readings meet in his story: the water of rebirth, and a life of thankful love.
study: Titus 3:3 recalls what we were before grace. How does remembering my own past make me gentler with others?
For what healing in my life have I not yet turned back to give thanks?

lead: Paul writes a personal letter to ask a Christian master to receive his runaway slave as a brother. In the Gospel Jesus says that the kingdom of God is already “among you”, though the Son of Man must first suffer. Where Christ reigns, people who were divided are made brothers.

r.h: No longer as a slave but as a brother
set: Philemon was a Christian of Colossae in whose house the Church met (v. 2). His slave Onesimus had left him, perhaps after some loss or wrong (v. 18), and had come to Paul, who was in prison. There Onesimus became a Christian. Paul sends him back with this short letter, the most personal in the New Testament.
str: v. 7: thanks for Philemon’s love.
vv. 8–14: Paul appeals, not commands, for Onesimus his “child”.
vv. 15–17: receive him “no longer as a slave” but as a beloved brother.
vv. 18–20: “charge that to my account”.
kw: The name Onesimus means “useful”. Paul plays on it in v. 11: once useless to you, now useful to you and to me. In v. 20 he plays on it again: “let me have this benefit (onaimēn) from you”.
Literally the inner parts, the seat of deep feeling. It appears in vv. 7, 12 and 20: Paul sends Onesimus as “my own heart”.
vv: I am appealing to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I have become during my imprisonment.
Paul fathered him in faith while in chains. The prisoner gives new life.
no longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother
Paul does not attack the law of the time directly; he places Philemon and Onesimus in a new relationship that makes the old one impossible to live in the same way.
If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.
Paul takes the debt on himself. Christians have long seen here a picture of Christ, who takes our debts on himself.
ch: The Catechism cites Philemon 16 when it teaches that it is a sin against human dignity to treat persons as merchandise or to enslave them (CCC 2414). The letter shows how the Gospel changes society from within: by changing the way brothers see each other.

r.h: The kingdom of God is among you
set: Some Pharisees ask Jesus when the kingdom of God will come. Many expected it with visible signs. Jesus answers them, and then speaks to his disciples about the day of the Son of Man.
str: vv. 20–21: the kingdom does not come with signs to be watched; it is among you.
vv. 22–24: do not run after rumours; the day of the Son of Man will be like lightning.
v. 25: but first he must suffer and be rejected.
kw: Watching closely for signs, as one watches the sky. The kingdom cannot be tracked like that.

The Greek can mean either. The NRSV and POC say “among you”: the kingdom is present in Jesus himself, standing in their midst. The Latin Vulgate has “within you”, and many spiritual writers read it of the inner life. Both are true, but the first fits the context best.
The word of divine necessity: the Son of Man “must” suffer. The way to glory passes through the Cross.
vv: For, in fact, the kingdom of God is among you.
But first he must endure much suffering and be rejected by this generation.
ch: The Catechism, explaining the Lord’s Prayer, recalls St Cyprian’s words that Christ himself may be called the kingdom of God, for in him we shall reign (CCC 2816). The kingdom is among us wherever Christ is present: in his word, in the sacraments and in the brother we receive.

qa: Why did Paul not tell Philemon to release all slaves?

Paul wrote within a society he could not change by one letter. But he put a seed into it: a slave is a brother “in the flesh and in the Lord”. Over time the Church came to teach clearly that slavery is contrary to human dignity (CCC 2414).
rite: St Josaphat Kuntsevych (1580–1623) was a monk and then Archbishop of Polotsk in the Ruthenian Church, which had entered into communion with Rome. He worked for the unity of the Church and was killed at Vitebsk in 1623. Like Paul in Philemon, he sought reconciliation; today we pray for unity among all Christians.
study: Is there someone I find hard to receive “as a brother” or sister? What would Paul say to me?
Where do I see the kingdom of God “among” us in my parish?

lead: The Elder warns a Church against teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Jesus warns his disciples that the day of the Son of Man will come suddenly, as in the days of Noah and Lot. Both readings ask us to stay with what is true and not to cling to what is passing.

r.h: Abide in the teaching
set: The second letter of John is the shortest book of the New Testament with the third. The writer calls himself “the elder”. He writes to “the elect lady and her children” (v. 1), most likely a local Church and its members. Some had left the community and were teaching a false idea of Christ (compare 1 John 2:19).
str: vv. 4–6: joy, and the old commandment: love one another, and walk in his commandments.
v. 7: deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh.
vv. 8–9: be on guard; whoever abides in the teaching has the Father and the Son.
kw: The deceivers denied that the Son of God truly became man. The faith insists that the Word truly took our flesh.
Literally “going ahead”. The false teachers presented themselves as advanced. John says that whoever runs ahead of the teaching of Christ leaves God behind.
vv: And this is love, that we walk according to his commandments
Love and obedience are not two things. To love is to walk in his commandments, and his commandment is to love.
whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.
ch: The Catechism notes that the first heresies denied not so much Christ’s divinity as his true humanity, against which the Church insisted that the Son of God came in the flesh (CCC 465). The Incarnation is the ground of our faith in the sacraments, where Christ still reaches us through bodily signs.

r.h: Remember Lot’s wife
set: Jesus continues his teaching on the day of the Son of Man (17:22–37). He draws on two stories from Genesis: the flood (Genesis 6–8) and the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19).
str: vv. 26–30: in the days of Noah and of Lot, people went on with ordinary life until judgment came suddenly.
vv. 31–33: do not turn back; remember Lot’s wife; whoever tries to secure life will lose it.
vv. 34–35: one taken, the other left.
v. 37: “Where, Lord?” “Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.”

¶ The NRSV has no v. 36. A few manuscripts add “Two will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left” from Matthew 24:40, but the oldest do not have it. The POC numbers the verses without it, so its v. 36 is NRSV v. 37.
kw: Used of being taken along with someone. The saying stresses separation and suddenness, not a secret removal.
The word can mean either. The image is proverbial: the sign of death is plain to all. When the day comes, it will be unmistakable.
vv: Remember Lot’s wife.
She looked back at the burning city and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). Her heart stayed with what she was leaving.
Those who try to make their life secure will lose it, but those who lose their life will keep it.
ch: Eating, drinking, marrying and building are not sins. The danger is to live as if they were everything. The Catechism teaches that the Last Judgment will come when Christ returns in glory, and that only the Father knows the day and the hour (CCC 1040). The answer to that uncertainty is not fear but readiness.

qa: Does Luke 17:34–35 teach a secret “rapture”?
No. Jesus is describing the suddenness of his coming, which will separate people who seem alike outwardly. The Church teaches one glorious coming of Christ at the end (CCC 1038–1040).
study: What “Sodom” am I tempted to look back at with longing?
How can I keep the Incarnation, God truly in the flesh, at the heart of my faith?

lead: The Elder praises Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries, so that “we may become co-workers with the truth”. Jesus tells the parable of a widow who keeps asking a judge for justice, to teach his disciples “to pray always and not to lose heart”. Hospitality and prayer are both ways of persevering.

r.h: Co-workers with the truth
set: The third letter of John is a personal note from “the elder” to Gaius. Travelling preachers moved from Church to Church and depended on local Christians for food and lodging. Gaius had welcomed them; a leader called Diotrephes had refused them (vv. 9–10).
str: vv. 5–6: Gaius has acted faithfully towards the brothers, even strangers; send them on in a way worthy of God.
vv. 7–8: they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from unbelievers; we ought to support them.
kw: for the sake of the Name
The Greek has simply “for the Name”, meaning the name of Jesus. The NRSV says “for the sake of Christ”; the POC keeps “for his Name”.
Those who receive missionaries share in their work. Hospitality is a form of mission.
vv: Beloved, you do faithfully whatever you do for the friends, even though they are strangers to you
Therefore we ought to support such people, so that we may become co-workers with the truth.
ch: The early Church organised such hospitality carefully; the Didache, an early Christian handbook, gives rules for receiving travelling apostles and prophets (in substance). Today the same work goes on when parishes support missionaries, seminarians and those who preach the Gospel far from home.

r.h: Pray always and do not lose heart
set: This parable follows Jesus’ words about the day of the Son of Man (17:22–37). While the disciples wait for his coming, they must pray. Luke states the point at the start: “their need to pray always and not to lose heart”.
str: v. 1: the purpose of the parable.
vv. 2–5: a judge who fears no one, and a widow who keeps coming.
vv. 6–8a: the lesson: if even this judge gives in, how much more will God grant justice to his chosen ones.
v. 8b: the question: will the Son of Man find faith on earth?
kw: To grow weary and give up. Prayer is the opposite of giving up.
Literally a boxing word, to strike under the eye. The judge jokes that the widow will “give him a black eye” by her persistence.
To vindicate, to defend someone’s rights. Widows had no one to defend them; God is their defender (Psalm 68:5).
vv: Then Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray always and not to lose heart.
And yet, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?
The parable ends with a question for us. The danger is not that God will fail to answer, but that we will stop asking.
ch: The Catechism names this among the parables of prayer that Luke records, together with the friend at midnight and the Pharisee and the tax collector (CCC 2613). It also teaches that we are to “pray constantly”, because prayer is the life of the new heart (CCC 2742–2745).

qa: Is God like the unjust judge?
No. The parable argues from the lesser to the greater. If even an unjust judge gives way to persistence, how much more will a loving Father hear his children.
study: Whom could I welcome or support, so as to become a co-worker with the truth?
In what prayer have I lost heart? What would it mean to keep coming, like the widow?

lead: On the Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time, the second-to-last Sunday of the Church's year, the readings look toward the end of all things and ask how we should live while we wait. The woman of Proverbs fills ordinary days with faithful work and opens her hand to the poor. Paul tells the Thessalonians that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, so the children of light keep awake. In the Gospel a master entrusts his property to his servants and, after a long time, returns to settle accounts. Psalm 128 sings of the blessing on those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways.

One thread runs through all three: something is entrusted, and there is a time of waiting before the account is given. The capable wife is trusted by her husband (Proverbs 31:11); the Thessalonians have received the faith and must not fall asleep; the servants receive the talents. Fear in the wrong sense makes the third servant bury his gift. The fear of the Lord, in the right sense, makes the gift grow. Since 2017 this Sunday has also been the World Day of the Poor, and the readings fit it well: the gifts entrusted to us are meant to bear fruit, and the first fruit is mercy.

r.h: The woman who fears the Lord
set: Proverbs is a collection of Israel's wisdom, gathered over centuries and placed under the name of Solomon. The book ends with a poem of twenty-two verses (31:10–31) in praise of “a capable wife”. It is an acrostic: in Hebrew each verse begins with the next letter of the alphabet, from aleph to tav. The form itself says that this is praise from A to Z, a complete picture.

The book opened with Wisdom as a woman calling in the streets (Proverbs 1–9) and with the motto “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). It closes with a woman in whom wisdom has become daily life, and with the same fear of the Lord (31:30). So the poem is both a portrait of a real household and a picture of Wisdom herself living among people.
str: v. 10: the question: who can find such a woman? She is worth more than jewels.
vv. 11–12: her husband's trust; she does him good all her days.
v. 13: her work with wool and flax.
vv. 19–20: her hands at the spindle and, in the same breath, open to the poor.
vv. 30–31: the key: not charm or beauty but the fear of the Lord; let her works praise her in the gates.

¶ The lectionary leaves out the middle verses (trade, fields, a vineyard, clothing) but keeps the frame. Verses 19 and 20 are a pair in Hebrew: they use the two words for hand, yād and kap, in crossed order, and the same verb “to send out”. The hands that reach for the spindle are the hands that reach out to the needy.
kw: Ḥayil means strength, ability, even wealth or an army. The phrase could be rendered “a woman of strength” or “of worth”. Boaz uses the same words of Ruth (Ruth 3:11). The strength praised here is shown in work, wisdom and kindness.
Not terror but a reverent love that puts God first. It is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7; 9:10), and the Church counts it among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831).
The word of Ecclesiastes, “vanity of vanities”: a breath, a vapour. In v. 30 beauty is called hebel. It passes like a breath; reverence for God lasts.
vv: A capable wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels.
The question does not mean such women cannot be found. It means she is a gift, worth more than anything bought. Proverbs said the same of Wisdom: “She is more precious than jewels” (3:15).
She opens her hand to the poor, and reaches out her hands to the needy.
Her household is busy and prosperous, yet its door is open. Wisdom in Israel is never only private success; it includes care for the poor, the widow and the stranger.
Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised.
This is the key to the whole poem. Her skill, trade and strength all flow from one root: the fear of the Lord.
Give her a share in the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the city gates.
The city gate was where the elders sat in judgment (v. 23). Her works speak for her in public. Here the poem meets the Gospel: the master too will look at what was done with what was entrusted.
ch: The Church reads this poem first as praise of real women and of the dignity of their work in the home and in society. St John Paul II, in his apostolic letter Mulieris Dignitatem (1988), speaks of the “perfect woman” of Proverbs 31:10 as an irreplaceable support and source of spiritual strength for others (n. 30). Christian commentators also read the poem spiritually: St Bede, in a short work on this chapter, saw in the strong woman the Church, the bride of Christ, who clothes and feeds her children (in substance). Placed beside the parable of the talents, she becomes a model of the good servant: faithful in small daily things, generous to the poor, and rooted in the fear of the Lord.

r.h: Children of the light do not sleep
set: This is very likely the oldest writing of the New Testament, sent by Paul from Corinth around AD 50–51 to a young Church he had been forced to leave in haste (Acts 17:1–10). The Thessalonians had questions about the end. In 4:13–18 Paul answered their grief over those who had died. Now he turns to the question of when: “the times and the seasons”.
str: vv. 1–2: no need to write about dates; the day will come like a thief in the night.
v. 3: the false peace of those who say “peace and security”, and the sudden labour pains.
vv. 4–5: but you are children of light and of the day.
v. 6: so let us keep awake and be sober.
kw: Chronos is time measured by the clock; kairos is the right or decisive moment. Jesus said the same before his Ascension: “It is not for you to know the times or periods” (Acts 1:7).
An old prophetic phrase for the day God acts in judgment and salvation (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31). For Paul it is the day of Christ's coming.
Many scholars hear in this phrase an echo of Roman propaganda, which praised the peace and security of the empire. No human order can give the security that belongs to God alone.
The same verb Jesus uses: “Keep awake therefore” (Matthew 25:13). Christian watchfulness is not anxiety but alert, sober faith.
vv: For you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.
A thief does not announce his hour. The image comes from Jesus himself (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39). The point is readiness, not fear: the day will surprise the world, not those who are watching.
When they say, “There is peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman
Labour pains are sudden, but they are not meaningless: they announce a birth. The end is both judgment and the birth of a new creation (compare Romans 8:22).
for you are all children of light and children of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness.
To be “children of” something is a Hebrew way of saying that we belong to it. Baptism, which early Christians such as St Justin called “illumination”, makes us children of the day.
So then let us not fall asleep as others do, but let us keep awake and be sober
ch: The Church has never fixed a date for the end, and she warns against those who do. The Catechism teaches that since the Ascension Christ's coming in glory is imminent, even though “it is not for you to know the times or periods” (CCC 673), and that we know neither the moment of the consummation of the earth nor the way the universe will be transformed (CCC 1048). Watchfulness, then, is a way of living each day as children of light. Paul's next verse names its armour: “the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation” (5:8).

r.h: Enter into the joy of your master
set: This is the second of the three parables that close Jesus' last discourse in Matthew (chapters 24–25). The bridesmaids taught readiness; the talents teach faithful work during the waiting; the judgment of the nations (25:31–46) shows that the work is love for the least. Matthew wrote for a Church that had learned the master might be away “a long time” (v. 19).

A talent was not a coin but a weight of silver, worth about six thousand denarii. Since a denarius was a labourer's daily wage, one talent was the wages of many years, perhaps fifteen to twenty. Even the servant who received “only” one talent received a fortune. Our English word “talent”, meaning a natural gift, comes from this parable. Later Jewish law regarded burying money as the safest way to keep a deposit, so the third servant did what seemed prudent; the parable says that this caution was his failure.
str: vv. 14–15: the master entrusts his property, “to each according to his ability”, and goes away.
vv. 16–18: two servants trade at once; the third digs a hole.
v. 19: after a long time the master returns to settle accounts.
vv. 20–23: two reports and two identical words of praise.
vv. 24–27: the third servant and his fear; the master's reply.
vv. 28–30: the talent is taken and given; the worthless servant is cast out.
¶ The two faithful servants receive exactly the same words of praise, though one made five talents and the other two. What is rewarded is faithfulness, not the size of the result.
kw: A large weight of silver (see above). The amount shows how generous the master is.
From the same root as pistis, faith. The good servant can be trusted because he trusted his master.
The word suggests hesitating and shrinking back as much as idleness. Fear made the servant hold back.
“Enter into the joy of your master”: the reward is not only more responsibility but a share in the master's own happiness.
vv: to one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability.
The gifts differ, and that is not unjust. Each receives what he can carry, and each is trusted.
Well done, good and trustworthy slave; you have been trustworthy in a few things, I will put you in charge of many things; enter into the joy of your master.
Five talents are called “a few things”. Everything we receive in this life is small compared with what God wants to give.
so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here you have what is yours.

The servant's picture of his master (“a harsh man”, v. 24) is false. The false picture produces fear, and fear produces nothing. He hands back the gift unused, as if the relationship were only about not losing.
For to all those who have, more will be given, and they will have an abundance; but from those who have nothing, even what they have will be taken away.
This is not a rule of economics. In the life of grace a gift that is used grows, and a gift that is refused withers. Jesus said the same about hearing the word (13:12).
ch: The Fathers read the talents as all of God's gifts: natural abilities, the word of God, the grace of the sacraments. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this parable, said that the talents are whatever ability each one has, whether protection, money, teaching or anything else, and that whoever can help others and does not is like the man who buried his talent (in substance). St Gregory the Great saw in the five talents the gifts of the outward senses, in the two understanding and action, and warned that whoever has received understanding must use it to serve others (in substance). The Catechism teaches that talents are not distributed equally, so that each person needs others, and that these differences call for generosity, kindness and sharing (CCC 1936–1937). On the World Day of the Poor the parable has a plain meaning: what we have received, money, time, skill and faith, is given to be shared, and the next page of Matthew shows where the master expects to find its fruit: “just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (25:40).

qa: Is God a “harsh man” who reaps where he did not sow?

No. That is the third servant's picture of his master, and the parable shows it to be false: the master gave lavishly and rewarded generously. He answers the servant on his own terms (“You knew, did you…?”) to show that even his excuse condemns him. Fear of a harsh God is the root of the buried talent; trust in a generous God makes the gift grow.
Does the parable praise making money or charging interest?

Jesus often took his images from ordinary life, here from business, but the subject is the kingdom of heaven. The point is fruitfulness, not finance. The Church's teaching on the just use of goods is found elsewhere, and on this very Sunday she asks us to share with the poor.
Who is the “capable wife” of Proverbs?

First of all a real wife and mother, honoured for wise and generous work. The poem also gathers up the whole book: she is wisdom made visible in a household. Christian readers have also seen in her a picture of the Church, the bride of Christ.
rite: In the Roman calendar this is the Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time, the last before the Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe (22 November); Advent begins on 29 November. In these closing weeks the Church turns our eyes to the end of time and the return of Christ. Pope Francis instituted the World Day of the Poor in his apostolic letter Misericordia et Misera (2016) at the close of the Jubilee of Mercy, and set it on this Sunday, just before the feast of the King who will say, “you did it to me”. Many parishes share a meal with the poor, take up a collection or visit those in need. At Mass today the talent of the Gospel can take the shape of a hand opened, like the hand of the woman in Proverbs.
study: The woman of Proverbs is praised for faithful work in small, daily things. Which ordinary task of mine could become an act of the fear of the Lord?
Paul calls us “children of light”. What helps me to keep awake and sober in faith, and what lulls me to sleep?
What is the “talent” I am most tempted to bury, and what fear keeps it buried?
On the World Day of the Poor, what concrete step can my family or parish take this week to open our hand to the needy?

lead: In these last weeks of the year the weekday readings open the Book of Revelation. Today the risen Christ speaks to the churches of Asia and calls Ephesus back to the love it had at first. In the Gospel a blind beggar near Jericho cries out to the Son of David and receives his sight. Both readings are about seeing again: a Church that must remember what it has lost, and a man who prays, “Lord, let me see again.”

r.h: Remember the love you had at first
set: Revelation was written by a prophet named John, in exile on the island of Patmos “because of the word of God” (1:9), most likely near the end of the reign of the emperor Domitian (about AD 95), as St Irenaeus reports. It is addressed to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, in today's western Turkey. Its style is apocalyptic: visions, numbers and symbols that show history as God sees it. It was meant to be read aloud in the liturgical assembly, and its first aim is to strengthen Christians under pressure, not to give a timetable of the end.
str: 1:1–3: the title, and the first blessing on those who read, hear and keep.
1:4: greeting from the eternal God, from the seven spirits, and from Jesus Christ.
2:1–5: the first of the seven letters, to Ephesus: praise (vv. 2–3), reproach (v. 4), a call to repent (v. 5).
kw: Not a riddle but the drawing back of a curtain. It is “the revelation of Jesus Christ”: given by him and about him.
1:3 is the first of seven beatitudes in Revelation. The blessing rests on those who hear the word in the assembly and keep it.
The love of the early days of conversion, warm and generous. Ephesus has kept sound teaching and endurance, but its love has cooled.
vv: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of the prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and who keep what is written in it; for the time is near.
One reader, many hearers: this is the Church at prayer. The blessing is not for curiosity about the future but for keeping the word.
But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.
A church can work hard, endure much and test false teachers (vv. 2–3) and still lose the heart of the matter. Right teaching without love is not enough (compare 1 Corinthians 13:2).
Remember then from what you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first.
Three verbs: remember, repent, do. The way back is not a new feeling but the old works of love taken up again. The lampstand is the church itself (1:20); without love it loses its place.
ch: The Catechism speaks of a “second conversion”, an uninterrupted task for the whole Church, which is holy and yet always in need of purification (CCC 1428). The letter to Ephesus is that call in miniature. Since seven is the number of fullness, the seven letters have long been read as words to the whole Church in every age: each of us may hear in them what the Spirit is saying today.

r.h: Lord, let me see again
set: Jesus is on his last journey to Jerusalem. Just before this he has foretold his Passion for the third time, and Luke notes that the Twelve “understood nothing about all these things” (18:34). Then, at Jericho, a blind man sees what they do not: he calls Jesus “Son of David” and asks for sight. Mark gives his name, Bartimaeus, and places the healing as Jesus leaves Jericho (Mark 10:46); Luke places it on the approach, so that it leads straight into the story of Zacchaeus.
str: vv. 35–37: the beggar hears the crowd: “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.”
vv. 38–39: he cries out, is told to be quiet, and cries out all the more.
vv. 40–42: Jesus stops, asks, and heals.
v. 43: he follows Jesus, glorifying God, and all the people praise God.
kw: A messianic title: the promised king of David's line (2 Samuel 7:12–16). The crowd says “of Nazareth”; the blind man sees more and says “Son of David”.
The verb can mean to regain sight or to look up. He asks for eyes and receives a new way of seeing.
“Your faith has saved you”: the same verb means to heal and to save. The healing of the body is a sign of salvation.
vv: Then he shouted, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
A short prayer from a man who has nothing: a name, a title and a cry for mercy.
Jesus stood still and ordered the man to be brought to him
The crowd on its way to Jerusalem would not stop for a beggar. Jesus stops.
Immediately he regained his sight and followed him, glorifying God
Healed, he does not go home; he follows Jesus on the road to Jerusalem, the road of the Cross.
ch: The Catechism counts the cry of the blind among the prayers Jesus answered during his ministry (CCC 2616), and it sees in the invocation of the holy name of Jesus, joined to the cry for mercy, the simplest way of praying always; from it grew the “Jesus Prayer”, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us sinners” (CCC 2667–2668). Every Mass begins with the same cry: “Lord, have mercy.” St Augustine, preaching on the blind men by the road, noted that the crowd tried to silence them, as the noise of the world, and even careless Christians, may try to silence our prayer; the answer is to cry out all the more (in substance).

qa: Was the healing on the way into Jericho or out of it?

Mark and Matthew place it as Jesus leaves Jericho, Luke as he approaches. The evangelists arrange events to teach, and Luke puts this healing first so that two stories at Jericho, a blind beggar and a rich tax collector, show the same truth: Jesus seeks the lost. Some have also pointed out that there were two Jerichos, the old town and Herod's new city nearby. The substance of the event is the same in all three Gospels.
study: What was my “first love” for Christ, and which “first works” could I take up again?
Where do I need to pray, like the blind man, “Lord, let me see again”?

lead: The letters to Sardis and Laodicea are among the sharpest in Revelation: a church that seems alive but is dead, and a church that is lukewarm and thinks it needs nothing. Yet the letter ends with Christ knocking at the door and asking to share a meal. In the Gospel he does exactly that at Jericho: he invites himself into the house of Zacchaeus, and salvation comes to it. Today is also the memorial of St Elizabeth of Hungary, who, like Zacchaeus, gave her goods to the poor.

r.h: I am standing at the door, knocking
set: Sardis had once been the rich capital of the kingdom of Lydia. Its citadel stood on a steep hill and was thought impossible to take, yet it was captured by surprise more than once because its guards did not keep watch. The warning “I will come like a thief” would have been felt there.

Laodicea was a wealthy city of banking, of fine black wool and of a well-known school of medicine. When an earthquake struck in AD 60, it rebuilt itself without help from Rome, as the historian Tacitus records. Its water came by aqueduct and arrived tepid, unlike the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis or the cold water of Colossae. Each detail of the letter touches the city's pride: rich, well clothed, with eye medicine, and lukewarm.
str: 3:1–3: Sardis: a name of being alive, but dead; wake up, remember, repent.
3:4–6: the faithful few in white; the book of life.
3:14–17: Laodicea: neither cold nor hot; “I am rich”.
3:18–20: Christ's counsel: gold, white robes, salve; then the knock at the door.
3:21–22: the promise of a place with him on his throne.
kw: Neither the healing heat of a hot spring nor the refreshment of cold water: useless, and so spat out. The fault is not a lack of feeling but complacency.
The word for the main evening meal. In the East, to share a table is to share life.
Each letter ends with a promise to the one who conquers. The victory is first Christ's (3:21) and is shared through faithfulness.
vv: you have a name of being alive, but you are dead.
A reputation can outlive the reality. Activity and fame are not the same as life in Christ.
For you say, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing.’ You do not realize that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.
The most dangerous poverty is the one we do not see. Christ offers what money cannot buy: faith refined by fire, the white garment of baptism, and eyes that see.
Listen! I am standing at the door, knocking; if you hear my voice and open the door, I will come in to you and eat with you, and you with me.

The letter that began with the threat to spit out ends with a knock. Christ does not break the door down. Many readers have heard here a call to the Eucharistic table. Holman Hunt's famous painting The Light of the World shows the door with no handle on the outside: it can be opened only from within.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in prayer God's initiative of love always comes first, and our prayer is a response (CCC 2567). Revelation 3:20 is that initiative in a single image. The Catechism also names lukewarmness, with indifference and acedia, among the sins against the love of God (CCC 2094). The remedy is not effort alone but opening the door: “Be earnest, therefore, and repent” (3:19).

r.h: Today salvation has come to this house
set: Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich city on the trade road from the east, with Herod's winter palace and groves of balsam and palm. It was a natural place for collecting tolls. Zacchaeus was a “chief tax collector”, a man who had bought the right to collect taxes and had others working under him. Such men were despised as collaborators with Roman power and as cheats. His name comes from the Hebrew for “pure” or “innocent”, which in the town's eyes he was not.
str: vv. 1–4: Zacchaeus wants to see who Jesus is and climbs a tree.
vv. 5–7: Jesus looks up and invites himself; the crowd grumbles.
vv. 8–10: Zacchaeus' promise and Jesus' declaration.
kw: A word Luke loves: “to you is born this day” (2:11), “Today this scripture has been fulfilled” (4:21), “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). Salvation is not only future; it comes now, when Christ is welcomed.
“I must stay at your house today.” Luke uses the same small word for the divine necessity of the Passion (9:22). This visit is part of God's plan.
The sycomore fig, a tree with a short trunk and low, wide branches, easy to climb. A rich official climbing a tree like a boy shows how much he wanted to see.
vv: He was trying to see who Jesus was
It begins with curiosity. Jesus can use even a small desire to see him.
Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today.
Zacchaeus wanted to see Jesus; it turns out that Jesus was looking for him. Jesus calls him by name before he has said a word of repentance.
Look, half of my possessions, Lord, I will give to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I will pay back four times as much.

The Law required repaying what was taken plus a fifth (Numbers 5:6–7); fourfold was the penalty for a stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1). Zacchaeus goes far beyond what the Law demands. Joy at being welcomed overflows into justice and generosity.
For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.
A summary of Luke's whole Gospel. It recalls God's promise as shepherd: “I will seek the lost” (Ezekiel 34:16).
ch: The Catechism points to Zacchaeus as the model of restitution: justice requires that what was unjustly taken be given back (CCC 2412). St Augustine, reading the tree's name as “foolish fig”, saw in it a figure of the Cross, which the world thinks foolish (1 Corinthians 1:23); whoever wants to see Jesus must climb it (in substance). The story shows the order of grace: Jesus' welcome comes first, conversion follows, and its fruit is love for the poor.

qa: Did Zacchaeus earn salvation by his generosity?

No. Jesus calls him and enters his house before he promises anything. His generosity is the response to grace, the sign that salvation has come. Some scholars read his words as a description of what he already did rather than a new promise; either way, the initiative is Jesus'.
rite: Today the Latin Church keeps the memorial of St Elizabeth of Hungary (1207–1231). A king's daughter, married young to Louis of Thuringia, she was known for her care of the poor, the sick and the hungry. After her husband died on his way to the crusade, she left court life, joined the Franciscan penitents, and spent her last years serving the sick in a hospital she founded at Marburg. She died at twenty-four and was canonised in 1235. Like Zacchaeus, she understood that wealth received from God is meant to pass into the hands of the poor.
study: Where am I tempted to say, like Laodicea, “I need nothing”?
Zacchaeus' joy turned at once into generosity. What would “half of my possessions” look like in my life today?

lead: After the letters, Revelation lifts its eyes: a door stands open in heaven, and John sees the throne of God surrounded by worship that never ends. In the Gospel, near Jerusalem, Jesus tells of a nobleman who goes away to receive royal power and entrusts money to his servants. Heaven worships the King now; on earth his servants work faithfully until he returns. Psalm 150, the last great Hallelujah of the Psalter, answers both.

r.h: Holy, holy, holy
set: Chapters 4 and 5 are the centre of the book's vision. Before any seal is opened or trumpet sounded, John is shown that God is on the throne. Christians in Asia lived under an emperor who liked to be acclaimed as lord and god; the historian Suetonius reports that Domitian wished to be called “our lord and god”. Here that acclamation is given to the Creator alone (4:11). The scene draws on Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1. Many interpreters see in the twenty-four elders the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, the whole people of God of both covenants (compare 21:12–14).
str: v. 1: an open door in heaven and the call, “Come up here.”
vv. 2–3: the throne and the One seated on it, shining like jewels, with a rainbow.
vv. 4–6a: twenty-four elders, lightning and thunder, seven torches, a sea of glass.
vv. 6b–8: four living creatures and their song.
vv. 9–11: the elders cast their crowns before the throne and sing to the Creator.
kw: The key word of the chapter. History may look like chaos, but the throne is not empty.
The song of the seraphim in Isaiah 6:3. To say “holy” three times is the strongest way of speaking in Hebrew: God is utterly other and utterly pure.
A word used in public acclamations. The Creator alone is worthy of glory and honour; in chapter 5 the same word will be sung to the Lamb.
vv: After this I looked, and there in heaven a door stood open!
In 3:20 Christ knocked at our door. Now heaven's door is opened to us. Worship is where the two doors meet.
Day and night without ceasing they sing, “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God the Almighty, who was and is and is to come.”
Isaiah's song with a new line: God is Lord of past, present and future. At every Mass the Church joins this song in the Sanctus.
they cast their crowns before the throne
The elders have crowns, but they do not keep them. Whatever glory we receive is returned to God.
ch: The Catechism draws on this chapter to describe the heavenly liturgy: “a throne stood in heaven, with one seated on the throne”, and all creation gathered in praise around him (CCC 1137–1139). The Second Vatican Council teaches that in the earthly liturgy we take part, by a foretaste, in the heavenly liturgy (Sacrosanctum Concilium 8). The Fathers took the four living creatures, a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle, as symbols of the four evangelists; the arrangement that became usual in the West, man for Matthew, lion for Mark, ox for Luke and eagle for John, comes from St Jerome.

r.h: Do business with these until I come back
set: Luke gives the reason for the parable: Jesus was near Jerusalem, and the people “supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately” (v. 11). The story corrects that hope: the king must first go away and then return.

The parable recalls real events. When Herod the Great died (4 BC), his son Archelaus went to Rome to have his kingship confirmed by Augustus, and a delegation of Jews followed him to oppose it, as the historian Josephus reports. Archelaus later rebuilt the royal palace at Jericho, where Jesus has just been. Luke's hearers would have caught the allusion.
str: v. 11: the occasion.
vv. 12–14: a nobleman leaves to receive royal power; ten servants receive a pound each; his citizens reject him.
vv. 15–19: he returns; two servants report ten and five pounds and receive cities.
vv. 20–26: the third servant and the cloth; the rule of having and not having.
vv. 27–28: the enemies judged; Jesus goes up to Jerusalem.
kw: A sum of a hundred denarii, about a hundred days' wages: far less than Matthew's talents. Here each servant receives the same, which points to a gift common to all, such as the word of the Gospel or the life of faith.
The gift is not to be wrapped up and stored; it must be put to work.
The same Greek word means kingdom and kingship. The nobleman goes away to receive the kingship that Jesus receives through his Passion, Resurrection and Ascension.
vv: Do business with these until I come back.
This is the time of the Church: between the King's going and his return.
Because you have been trustworthy in a very small thing, take charge of ten cities.
A pound for ten cities: the reward is out of all proportion to the work. Compare 16:10: “Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.”
After he had said this, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
The parable ends and the real story begins. The King goes ahead of his disciples to the city where he will be crowned with thorns.
ch: The parable warns against two errors: thinking that the kingdom will come at once, without the Cross and the long time of the Church, and thinking that the time of waiting is a time to do nothing. The Catechism teaches that Christ's reign is already present in the Church, yet is still to be fulfilled “with power and great glory” at the King's return (CCC 671). The harsh last verse belongs to the story of an earthly king; Jesus himself will soon weep over the city that does not receive him (19:41). The judgment is real, but the heart of the true King is shown on the Cross.

qa: How is this parable different from the talents in Matthew?

They are related but not the same. In Matthew the servants receive different sums according to ability; in Luke each receives one pound, and a second thread is added: citizens who reject the king. Matthew stresses the use of varied gifts; Luke stresses faithfulness with the one gift common to all, and the rejection of the King on his way to Jerusalem.
study: When I take part in Mass, do I remember that I join the song of heaven, “Holy, holy, holy”?
What is the “pound” the Lord has given to every Christian, and how am I putting it to work?

lead: Yesterday's vision of the throne continues: in God's right hand is a sealed scroll, and no one can open it until the Lamb who was slaughtered comes forward. In the Gospel Jesus comes near Jerusalem and weeps over the city that did not recognise the time of its visitation. The Lamb who opens the meaning of history is the same Lord who weeps over those who will not receive his peace. Psalm 149 sings the new song of the faithful.

r.h: Worthy is the Lamb
set: The scroll in God's right hand holds his plan for history and its judgment. It is written on both sides, like the scroll Ezekiel saw (Ezekiel 2:9–10), and sealed with seven seals, that is, completely closed. The question of the chapter is who can open it: who can make sense of history and bring it to its goal.
str: vv. 1–4: the sealed scroll; no one is worthy; John weeps.
v. 5: an elder announces the Lion of Judah, the Root of David.
vv. 6–7: John sees a Lamb standing as if slaughtered, who takes the scroll.
vv. 8–10: the living creatures and the elders fall down and sing a new song.
kw: Revelation calls Christ the Lamb about thirty times. The title recalls the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) and the servant led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7).
A sacrificial word. The Lamb is standing, that is, risen, yet he bears the marks of his death. The glorified Christ keeps his wounds (compare John 20:27).
The language of the market where slaves were bought. Christ's blood paid the price that made us God's own.
vv: See, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered
John hears “Lion”: the messianic titles of Genesis 49:9 and Isaiah 11:1, 10.
Then I saw between the throne and the four living creatures and among the elders a Lamb standing as if it had been slaughtered
He turns and sees a Lamb. This is the heart of the book: the victory of the Lion is the self-giving of the Lamb. God conquers by love that suffers.
for you were slaughtered and by your blood you ransomed for God saints from every tribe and language and people and nation; you have made them to be a kingdom and priests serving our God
Four words for humanity describe a Church gathered from every people. The redeemed share Christ's royal priesthood (Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:9).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the whole community of believers is priestly, sharing in Christ's priesthood through baptism, and it cites these verses (CCC 1546). At every Mass the priest shows the Host and says, “Behold the Lamb of God… Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb,” joining the words of John the Baptist (John 1:29) to the wedding feast of the Lamb in Revelation (19:9). The golden bowls of incense, “which are the prayers of the saints” (5:8), show that the prayers of the Church on earth rise before God's throne.

r.h: If you had only recognized the things that make for peace
set: Jesus has come down the Mount of Olives amid the praise of his disciples (19:37–40). As the city comes into view, the shouts give way to tears. Only Luke records this weeping. A small church on the Mount of Olives called Dominus Flevit (“the Lord wept”), built in the shape of a tear, marks the place by tradition. About forty years later, in AD 70, the Roman army under Titus surrounded Jerusalem with a siege wall and destroyed the city and the Temple, as Josephus describes.
str: v. 41: Jesus sees the city and weeps.
v. 42: the lament: if only you had known the things that make for peace.
vv. 43–44: the siege foretold, and its cause: the time of visitation was not recognised.
kw: Luke uses the word for loud weeping, not quiet tears. The King who is being acclaimed weeps for those who will reject him.
The name Jerusalem was popularly heard as “city of peace” (shalom). The city of peace does not see the things that make for peace.
God's coming to save. Zechariah sang that God “has looked favorably on his people” (1:68); now God visits them in Jesus himself.
vv: As he came near and saw the city, he wept over it
Like Jeremiah before him (Jeremiah 9:1), Jesus mourns for his own city. His prophecy is a lament, not a curse.
If you, even you, had only recognized on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.
because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.
The tragedy is not that God did not come, but that his coming was not recognised.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse with great care: “Jerusalem did not recognize the time of her visitation”, and adds at once that the Jews remain most dear to God for the sake of their fathers, and that what happened in Christ's Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). The tears of Jesus are a warning to every disciple and every Church: the day of visitation is always “this day”, and anyone can miss the things that make for peace.

study: The Lion conquers as a Lamb. Where am I tempted to seek victory by force rather than by self-giving love?
What are “the things that make for peace” in my family or community today, and am I recognising them?

lead: John is told to take a little scroll and eat it: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach. The word of God is a joy to receive and a cost to proclaim. In the Gospel Jesus cleanses the Temple and then teaches there every day, while the people hang on his words. Both readings are about the word: eaten, taught and heard. The psalm (Psalm 119) sings, “How sweet are your words to my taste.”

r.h: Take it, and eat
set: Between the sixth and the seventh trumpets Revelation pauses. A mighty angel comes down with a little open scroll, and John's call as a prophet is renewed. The scene recalls the call of Ezekiel, who was given a scroll to eat and found it “as sweet as honey” (Ezekiel 3:3), but then went away “in bitterness” (Ezekiel 3:14). Jeremiah too could say, “Your words were found, and I ate them” (Jeremiah 15:16).
str: v. 8: the voice from heaven: go and take the scroll.
vv. 9–10: eating the scroll: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach.
v. 11: the mission: prophesy again about many peoples.
kw: A diminutive. It is a message given for this moment, open, not sealed like the scroll of chapter 5.
The word is sweet because it is God's; it is bitter because it brings judgment, and suffering to those who carry it.
vv: Take it, and eat; it will be bitter to your stomach, but sweet as honey in your mouth.
The prophet must not only read the word but take it into himself. What he proclaims must first become part of him.
You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.
The mission is universal. The word is not eaten for private enjoyment; it is eaten to be preached.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church has always venerated the divine Scriptures as she venerates the Body of the Lord, offering the faithful the bread of life from the one table of the word of God and of the Body of Christ (Dei Verbum 21; CCC 103). The ancient practice of lectio divina speaks of chewing the word slowly, as John eats the scroll. Revelation 10 adds a realistic note: the word that delights also wounds, because it asks us to change and to bear witness.

r.h: My house shall be a house of prayer
set: Jesus enters Jerusalem and goes straight to the Temple. In its outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, animals were sold for the sacrifices and coins were changed for the Temple tax. Luke tells the cleansing very briefly and then shows Jesus teaching in the Temple every day. His action is a prophetic sign: the Temple is to be a place of prayer and of teaching, the house of his Father (2:49).
str: v. 45: he drives out the sellers.
v. 46: the word of Scripture, from Isaiah and Jeremiah.
vv. 47–48: daily teaching; the leaders seek to kill him; the people hang on his words.
kw: From Isaiah 56:7, where God says that his house shall be called a house of prayer “for all peoples”.
From Jeremiah's sermon at the Temple gate (Jeremiah 7:11). A den is where robbers hide after their crimes; Jeremiah's charge was that worship had become a hiding place for injustice.
Literally “they were hanging on him”, listening. The people cling to his words.
vv: It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers.
Jesus calls the Temple “my house”. He speaks as the Son in his Father's house.
Every day he was teaching in the temple.
After the cleansing comes the teaching. The house of prayer is filled with the word.
for all the people were spellbound by what they heard.
The leaders cannot act against him because of the people. Luke distinguishes the leaders, who plot, from the people, who listen gladly.
ch: The Catechism explains that Jesus went up to the Temple as the privileged place of encounter with God, the dwelling of his Father and a house of prayer, and that he was angered because its outer court had become a place of commerce (CCC 583–584). St Paul teaches that Christians are now God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). The cleansing calls us to keep both our churches and our hearts as houses of prayer, where the word of Jesus is heard.

study: Is the word of God “sweet” to me? Do I also accept its “bitter” part, when it asks me to change?
What needs to be cleansed in the temple of my own heart so that it may be a house of prayer?

lead: On the memorial of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the readings speak of the life that God gives. In Revelation two witnesses are killed, but after three and a half days “the breath of life from God” enters them and they rise. In the Gospel Jesus answers the Sadducees: God is “God not of the dead, but of the living; for to him all of them are alive.” Psalm 144 blesses the Lord, our Rock.

r.h: The breath of life from God entered them
set: Chapter 11 tells of two witnesses who prophesy for 1,260 days, that is 42 months or three and a half years, the symbolic time of persecution taken from Daniel (Daniel 7:25). Their powers recall Elijah, who shut the sky (1 Kings 17:1) and called down fire (2 Kings 1:10), and Moses, who turned water into blood (Exodus 7:20). Some early writers, such as St Hippolytus, thought they were Enoch and Elijah returning at the end; many modern interpreters see in them the witnessing Church, two in number because the Law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).
str: v. 4: the two olive trees and the two lampstands.
vv. 5–6: their power while they prophesy.
vv. 7–10: the beast kills them; their bodies lie in the street; the world rejoices.
vv. 11–12: the breath of life; they stand up and are taken up in a cloud.
kw: The word that came to mean “martyr”: one whose witness is sealed with blood.
The language of Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:5, 10) and of God's breath in Genesis 2:7. God's Spirit raises the dead.
From Zechariah 4, where two olive trees supply oil to the lampstand: “the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:14).
vv: These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
Olive trees give oil, lampstands give light. Witnesses are anointed by God in order to give light to the world.
their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that is prophetically called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.
The witnesses share their Lord's fate. The “great city” is not one place on the map but every city that sets itself against God.
But after the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet
As Christ rose on the third day, so his witnesses rise. The last word belongs not to the beast but to God.
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith, a witness even unto death (CCC 2473). This reading is the story of every martyr: rejected, silenced, apparently defeated, and raised by God. Its call, “Come up here!” (11:12), echoes the call to John in 4:1 and the Ascension of the Lord: those who bear witness are promised a share in his victory.

r.h: He is God not of the dead, but of the living
set: The Sadducees were a party of priestly and wealthy families linked with the Temple. They held to the written Law of Moses and rejected the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). Their question uses the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10): if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow so that the dead man's name would not be lost. The case of seven brothers is meant to make the resurrection look absurd. It may echo the story of Sarah in the Book of Tobit, who had lost seven husbands (Tobit 3:8).
str: vv. 27–33: the Sadducees' question.
vv. 34–36: Jesus' first answer: the life of the resurrection is not a copy of this life.
vv. 37–38: his second answer, from Moses himself: the burning bush.
vv. 39–40: some scribes approve; no one dares to ask more.
kw: Literally “standing up again”. Not a return to the same earthly life, but entry into the life of “that age”.
A word found only here in the New Testament. It does not mean that the risen become angels, but that, like the angels, they no longer die, and so no longer marry to continue the human race.
A Semitic way of saying: those who belong to the resurrection, whose life comes from it.
vv: but those who are considered worthy of a place in that age and in the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.
Jesus does not despise marriage; he says that the life to come is greater than this one. Love is not lost; it is fulfilled in God.
And the fact that the dead are raised Moses himself showed, in the story about the bush, where he speaks of the Lord as the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.
Jesus answers from the Torah, which the Sadducees accepted (Exodus 3:6). God does not call himself the God of the dead. If he is still their God, they are alive to him.
Now he is God not of the dead, but of the living; for to him all of them are alive.

The last phrase is found only in Luke. Our hope rests above all on the faithfulness of God, who does not abandon those he loves; even the immortality of the soul is his gift, and he will raise the body too.
ch: The Catechism recalls this debate when it teaches the resurrection of the dead: to the Sadducees who denied it, Jesus answered that they knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, and faith in the resurrection rests on faith in God, who “is not God of the dead, but of the living” (CCC 993). The Church also sees in consecrated virginity a sign of the world to come, where they “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (CCC 1619).

qa: Will husbands and wives know each other in heaven?

Jesus says that the risen do not marry, because the life to come is not a continuation of earthly institutions. He does not say that persons or love are forgotten. The Church hopes for heaven as a perfect communion of life and love with the Holy Trinity, with the Virgin Mary, the angels and all the blessed (CCC 1024), in which every bond of true love is purified and fulfilled.
rite: Today's memorial of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary comes from the East, where it is linked with the dedication of the New Church of St Mary in Jerusalem in 543. Its story, Mary brought as a child to the Temple and offered to God, comes from the ancient Protoevangelium of James, not from the Bible. St Paul VI kept the memorial because, despite its legendary details, it presents lofty and exemplary values: Mary's whole life given to God (Marialis Cultus 8). She who belonged wholly to God is the first of the “children of the resurrection”, taken body and soul into glory. Today is also Pro Orantibus Day, when the Church prays for cloistered contemplative communities, who like Mary have given their lives to God in prayer.
study: The two witnesses were raised by “the breath of life from God”. Where do I need God's breath to raise what has died in me?
Mary gave her whole life to God from her youth. What difference does it make to my life that God is “God not of the dead, but of the living”?

lead: On the last Sunday of the Church's year the readings show us what kind of king Christ is. In Ezekiel, God himself promises to be the shepherd of his scattered flock, seeking the lost and healing the injured, and also judging between sheep and sheep. The psalm answers with the prayer every Christian knows: “The Lord is my shepherd.” In First Corinthians, Christ the risen one reigns until every enemy is overcome, the last being death, and then hands the kingdom to the Father so that God may be all in all. In Matthew, the Son of Man sits on his throne as king and shepherd, and judges the nations by one measure: what they did to the least of his brothers and sisters.

The line runs from shepherd to king to judge, and the three are one person. The King of the universe does not rule from a distance. He looks for the lost sheep, he goes down into death to destroy it, and at the end he is found hidden in the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner. The key words are seeking, reigning and recognising.

r.h: I myself will be the shepherd
set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the first group of exiles in 597 BC. He spoke to the exiles before and after the fall of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC. Chapter 34 comes just after the news reaches him that the city has fallen (33:21). The question in everyone's mind is why the nation collapsed, and whether God has abandoned his people.

In the ancient Near East kings were commonly called shepherds; Hammurabi of Babylon calls himself a shepherd in the prologue to his laws. So when Ezekiel speaks against “the shepherds of Israel” (34:2), he means the kings and leaders who fed themselves and not the flock. Today's reading begins at the turning point: since the human shepherds have failed, God will shepherd his sheep himself.
str: vv. 1–10 (not read): the charge against the shepherds who fed themselves, and God's sentence on them.
vv. 11–12: God himself searches for his scattered sheep and rescues them from the “day of clouds and thick darkness”.
vv. 13–14 (omitted today): he gathers them from the nations and feeds them on the mountains of Israel.
vv. 15–16: God shepherds, gives rest, seeks, brings back, binds up and strengthens.
v. 17: he judges between sheep and sheep.

¶ The chapter goes on to promise “one shepherd, my servant David” (34:23). God himself will shepherd, and yet a son of David will shepherd. The two promises meet only in Christ, who is both God and the Son of David.
kw: From the verb rā‘āh, to pasture, to feed. A shepherd in the Bible is the one who feeds. The failed shepherds fed themselves (34:2); God feeds the flock (34:14–15).
The same verb is used for seeking God in prayer. Here it is turned around: it is God who goes looking for his people.
“I will feed them with justice” (v. 16). God's care is not soft indulgence. It sets things right, and so it includes judgment (v. 17).
vv: I myself will search for my sheep, and will seek them out.
“I myself” is emphatic in Hebrew. After the failure of the kings, God does not send a better official; he comes himself. This is the seed of the Incarnation.
I will rescue them from all the places to which they have been scattered on a day of clouds and thick darkness.
“A day of clouds and thick darkness” is the language of the day of the Lord (Joel 2:2; Zephaniah 1:15). Here it describes the disaster of 587. God goes into the darkness to bring his sheep out.
I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak, but the fat and the strong I will destroy. I will feed them with justice.

Each verb answers a charge in 34:4, where the bad shepherds did none of these things. A note on the text: the Hebrew has “I will destroy” the fat and the strong, which the NRSV follows. The Greek Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate read “I will watch over” them; the two Hebrew words look very alike. The Malayalam POC follows this second reading (സംരക്ഷിക്കും). The Hebrew fits v. 17, where the strong sheep that push the weak aside are judged (34:20–21).
I shall judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats:
Judgment does not fall only on the shepherds. Inside the flock too, some sheep trample the pasture and foul the water for others (34:18–19). This verse prepares directly for today's Gospel.
ch: Jesus takes this chapter to himself when he says, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11), and when he tells of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to look for the one lost sheep (Luke 15:4–7). The Catechism lists the sheepfold among the images of the Church, a flock of which God himself foretold that he would be the shepherd (CCC 754, citing Ezekiel 34). St Augustine's sermon “On the Shepherds” is a long commentary on this chapter: those who lead in the Church must feed the flock and not themselves, and all of them are sheep of the one Shepherd (in substance).

r.h: He must reign until death is destroyed
set: Paul wrote to the Church he had founded at Corinth from Ephesus, around AD 54. Chapter 15 answers some at Corinth who said “there is no resurrection of the dead” (15:12). They may have believed in a survival of the soul, but found a bodily resurrection foolish. Paul first recalls the creed he received, that Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared (15:3–8), and then shows that if Christ is raised, the dead will be raised too.
str: v. 20: Christ is raised as the first fruits.
vv. 21–22: one man brought death, one man brings resurrection: Adam and Christ.
v. 23: the order: Christ first, then at his coming those who belong to him.
vv. 24–26: the end: Christ hands over the kingdom after destroying every hostile power; the last enemy is death.
v. 27 (omitted): Psalm 8:6, “all things under his feet”.
v. 28: the Son himself will be subjected to the Father, so that God may be all in all.
kw: The first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge that the whole harvest belongs to him (Leviticus 23:10–11). Christ's resurrection is not an isolated event; it is the first part of a harvest that includes us.
The word for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Paul uses it for Christ's return in glory.
Used of every “ruler and authority and power” and of death. In v. 26 the verb is in the present tense; many read this as saying that death is already being overcome.
The goal of all history: God's life filling everything and everyone, with nothing left outside it.
vv: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died.
After imagining a world without the resurrection (15:12–19), Paul turns with “But in fact”. The whole Christian hope rests on this fact.
for as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ.
Adam and Christ are two heads of humanity. We belong to Adam by birth and to Christ by faith and baptism. Paul develops the same contrast in Romans 5:12–21.
For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.
An echo of Psalm 110:1, the psalm the New Testament quotes more often than any other. Christ's reign is not only future; it has begun with his resurrection and is now at work.
The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
Death is called an enemy, not a friend or a natural release. Christ did not come to make us comfortable with death but to destroy it.
so that God may be all in all.
ch: Verse 28 was used by the Arians to argue that the Son is less than the Father. The Fathers answered that the Son is subject as man and as head of his body the Church; in his divinity he is equal to the Father. St Gregory of Nazianzus explains that Christ makes our subjection his own, as he made our sin and our curse his own (in substance). When Marcellus of Ancyra taught that Christ's kingdom would one day end, the Church added to the Creed at Constantinople in 381 the words we still say at Mass: “and his kingdom will have no end”.

The Catechism teaches that Christ's reign is already present in the Church but still to be fulfilled with power and great glory (CCC 671), and that at the end of time the Kingdom will come in its fullness and God will be “all in all” (CCC 1060).

r.h: You did it to me
set: This is the last scene of Jesus' last discourse in Matthew (chapters 24–25), and the last teaching before the Passion. Immediately after it Jesus says, “after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (26:2). The king who will judge the nations is about to be judged himself, stripped, thirsty and a prisoner.

It is not a parable in the strict sense but a great picture of the judgment, with one comparison inside it, the shepherd separating sheep from goats. In Palestine sheep and goats grazed together in mixed flocks; it is often explained that they were separated at evening, because goats need more warmth at night. The right hand is the place of honour.
str: vv. 31–33: the Son of Man comes in glory, the nations are gathered, sheep to the right and goats to the left.
vv. 34–40: the king speaks to those on his right; six works of mercy; their surprise; “you did it to me”.
vv. 41–45: the same pattern for those on his left: the same six needs, the same surprise, “you did not do it to me”.
v. 46: two ways out: eternal punishment, eternal life.
¶ The list of six needs is repeated four times. Matthew wants it learned by heart.
kw: The Son of Man of v. 31 becomes “the king” in v. 34. The one who sits on the throne of glory calls God “my Father”. This is the Gospel of the solemnity of Christ the King.
Every people is gathered, not Israel alone and not the Church alone. The Church reads the scene as the universal judgment of all humanity.

The superlative of “small”. In Matthew the “little ones” are often the disciples (10:42; 18:6), but the Church has always read the passage as including every person in need, with whom Christ identifies himself.
vv: When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory.
The language is from Daniel 7:13–14 and Zechariah 14:5. The poor rabbi from Nazareth speaks of himself as the judge of the world.
Come, you that are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world;

The kingdom was prepared “from the foundation of the world”. God's plan from the beginning was not judgment but blessing; the fire, by contrast, was prepared “for the devil and his angels” (v. 41), not for human beings.
Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and gave you food,

Both groups are surprised. The righteous did not help the poor in order to earn a reward from Christ; they simply helped. And those on the left would gladly have served Christ if they had recognised him.
Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.

The NRSV's “members of my family” renders the Greek “my brothers”. The king does not say “it is as if you did it to me” but “you did it to me”. Christ truly identifies himself with the poor and is met in them.
And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.
The same adjective, “eternal”, describes both. The Gospel takes our choices with full seriousness.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus identifies himself with the poor of every kind and makes active love toward them the condition for entering his kingdom (CCC 544). It quotes this passage when it teaches that we cannot be united with God if we fail to meet the serious needs of the poor and the little ones who are his brethren (CCC 1033). It also gives St John of the Cross's saying: at the evening of life we shall be judged on our love (CCC 1022).

St John Chrysostom warned his people not to honour Christ's body in church with silk vestments while neglecting him outside, cold and naked (in substance). Sulpicius Severus tells that after St Martin of Tours cut his cloak in two for a beggar at Amiens, Christ appeared to him in a dream wearing that half-cloak.

qa: Does this Gospel mean we are saved by good works, not by faith?

No. The works here are the fruit of a love that comes from God's grace. Faith that is real “works through love” (Galatians 5:6), and the Catechism teaches that grace comes first and our merit is itself God's gift (CCC 2008, 2011). Matthew shows what living faith looks like from the outside.
Is hell really eternal?

The Church teaches that hell exists and is eternal, and that its chief pain is eternal separation from God (CCC 1035). It is the result of a person's own deliberate and final refusal of love (CCC 1033). God predestines no one to hell (CCC 1037). The Gospel is a warning given in time, while there is still time.
Why are the goats on the left? Are goats bad?
No. In the picture, sheep and goats belong to the same shepherd and graze together. The comparison is only about separation. Goats were valuable animals, used for sacrifice like sheep.
rite: Pope Pius XI established the feast of Christ the King in 1925 with the encyclical Quas Primas, at a time when many nations were pushing God out of public life. He placed it on the last Sunday of October. In the reform after the Second Vatican Council, Pope Paul VI moved it to the last Sunday of the liturgical year and gave it its full title, “Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe”, so that the whole year now ends looking at Christ's coming in glory. Pius XI also asked that the consecration of the human race to the Sacred Heart of Jesus be renewed every year on this feast.

The Preface of the Mass describes the kingdom Christ will hand to the Father: a kingdom of truth and life, a kingdom of holiness and grace, a kingdom of justice, love and peace. Since 2021 this Sunday is also the diocesan celebration of World Youth Day. Next Sunday Advent begins, and the readings move from Matthew to Mark (Year B).
study: Ezekiel's God seeks the lost and binds up the injured. Who in my parish or family is “strayed” or “injured” today, and what can I do this week?
1 Corinthians 15:26 calls death an enemy. How does faith in the resurrection change the way a Christian family faces a funeral?
In Matthew 25 both groups are surprised. Why is it important that the righteous did not know they were serving Christ?
Which of the six works of mercy is hardest for me, and why?

lead: In the last week of the Church's year the weekday readings come from the end of the Book of Revelation and from Jesus' last discourse in Luke. Today they meet in two pictures of wholehearted belonging: the redeemed who “follow the Lamb wherever he goes”, and a poor widow who puts into the Temple treasury “all she had to live on”.

r.h: They follow the Lamb wherever he goes
set: Chapter 13 described two beasts, the powers that demand worship and put their mark on people's hands and foreheads. Chapter 14 answers with the opposite picture: the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with those who bear his name and the Father's name on their foreheads. Revelation was written to Churches in Asia Minor under pressure from the cult of the Roman emperor, probably in the 90s AD.
str: v. 1: the Lamb on Mount Zion and the 144,000 with his name.
vv. 2–3: a voice like many waters and harps; a new song only the redeemed can learn.
vv. 4b–5: who they are: followers of the Lamb, first fruits, without falsehood.
kw: John's favourite title for Christ, used about thirty times in Revelation. The Lamb “standing as if it had been slaughtered” (5:6) is the crucified and risen Christ.
Twelve times twelve times a thousand: the twelve tribes multiplied into a vast, complete people. In 7:9 the same people appear as “a great multitude that no one could count”.
